title: The parting word
hookLine: when I go from here, let this be my parting word: what I have seen is unsurpassable (Gitanjali 96)
tomorrow: why does a haiku tuck in a word for the season?

lines: A NOTE FOR WHOEVER FINDS IT.
cards: Some people leave a note in their phone for whoever finds it someday.
Tagore wrote his goodbye long before he needed it, in Gitanjali's ninety-sixth song: "When I go from hence let this be my parting word, that what I have seen is unsurpassable." Not a regret.
Not a warning to the rest of us. A thank-you, written while there was still plenty left to see. His biographers describe him in his last illness, still dictating poems from his bed.

teach.h: TWO ROADS: LEAVE IT, OR LOVE IT.
teach.b: That parting word picks a side in one of India's long arguments: when you seek God, or when you're leaving, what do you do with the world? One road is renunciation.
The sannyasi, the renouncer, gives up home, name and possessions, because attachment binds, and freedom means letting go. Its best case is strong. Tradition says the Buddha left a palace.
The Upanishads honor those who leave for the forest.
Whatever you cling to, you will lose; loosen your grip first, and you'll be free when it goes. The other road is Tagore's: delight.
In Gitanjali's seventy-third song he writes: "Deliverance is not for me in renunciation. I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight."

For him the world is God's own song, and the way out is all the way through: love what you see so fully that leaving becomes thanks. Its best case is strong too. Turning down a gift can look like turning away the giver.

Two roads, both walked by serious, loving people for a very long time, and both still walked today. And notice that Tagore's own goodbye keeps a little of each. When he goes, he does let go; he doesn't cling.
But he lets go saying that what he has seen could not be surpassed.

how: In Hindu life, sannyasa (renunciation) is a recognized path, often taken late in life; Tagore's songs, including Gitanjali's farewell songs, are read and sung at memorials in Bengal.

o: a last warning to those left behind
a goodbye that thanks the world
a will saying who inherits what

games.q: two roads at the end: tap the pairs.
p: what I have seen is unsurpassable
one who renounces home and possessions
still dictating poems from his bed

s: Tagore's parting word warns people about the world's dangers
it's a thank-you: what I have seen is unsurpassable.
renunciation has a serious case in Indian traditions
loosen your grip on what binds you, and you're free when it goes. the sannyasi walks that road.
Gitanjali condemns the renouncer's road as wrong for everyone
Tagore says deliverance is not for him in renunciation. he speaks for his own road.

games.q: your aunt, nearing retirement, plans to give away most of what she owns and live very simply. your cousin calls it running away from life. state your aunt's best case.
o: what you cling to binds you; letting go first can be its own freedom.
Tagore proved renouncing is wrong, so she ought to keep everything.
she'll save money, and that's the real reason anyone simplifies.
games.why: that's the renouncer's case, the road of sannyasa. Tagore chose bonds of delight, but he didn't call the other road foolish.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, and write one line by hand: something you've seen that nothing has topped. Keep it plain: a face, a view, a kitchen late at night.
Then sit with the line in front of you for the rest of the two minutes.

wordCard.voice: The parting word: Gitanjali ninety-six, Tagore's goodbye written in advance, saying that what he has seen of the world is unsurpassable. A farewell that is all thanks.

orig.note: Sanskrit: renunciation, giving up home and possessions for the spiritual life. The road Tagore didn't take.

carryVoice: Your line: what I have seen. Tagore's goodbye was a thank-you to the world. Until next time.
